{"id":"Q006_ubiquitin_like_function_divergence","track":"held_out","category":"functional_inference","prompt":"What biologically useful relationship does SCOPe support among ubiquitin-related proteins, UBX domains, and Ras-binding domains, and what annotation transfer would be unsafe?"}

item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q006_ubiquitin_like_function_divergence","answer":"SCOPe places ubiquitin-related proteins, Ras-binding domains/RBDs, and UBX domains as distinct families inside the same beta-Grasp, ubiquitin-like superfamily, d.15.1, rather than merely as unrelated proteins with a vaguely similar shape. The useful inference is therefore remote homology of the compact ubiquitin/beta-grasp scaffold across proteins that have diverged to do different jobs: canonical ubiquitin-like proteins are small protein modifiers or modifier-like domains, RBDs are Ras-family GTPase effector-binding modules, and UBX domains are ubiquitin-like domains used in adaptor proteins, notably in the p97/VCP system. The family split is the important limit. It would be unsafe to transfer a specific ubiquitin-conjugation or ubiquitin-like-modifier annotation to a Ras-binding domain or a UBX domain just because they are in d.15.1, and equally unsafe to call an arbitrary ubiquitin-related or UBX domain a Ras-binding effector domain from the shared fold/superfamily alone; at most the classification supports the shared beta-grasp core and a very broad protein-interaction propensity.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
